tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge the Record of a Case That Did Not End in Conviction (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(4))
tracks.publicName: Clearing a case that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 99-19-71(4), read from the enrolled text of 2026 HB 1546 which reenacts the whole section effective 1 July 2026, provides: 'Upon petition therefor, a justice, county, circuit or municipal court shall expunge the record of any case in which an arrest was made, the person arrested was released and the case was dismissed or the charges were dropped or there was no disposition of such case, or the person was found not guilty at trial.' Relief is MANDATORY on the statutory language — the court 'shall expunge' — which makes this one of very few mandatory record-clearing provisions in the country and the headline of the Mississippi product. There is no offence list, no waiting period, no completion requirement, no pending-charge restriction and no first-offender requirement in subsection (4). It is the broadest relief in Mississippi. Crucially, the one-felony-per-lifetime cap sits in subsection (2)(a) and applies to felony CONVICTION expungement only, so a participant who uses this track has not spent their one felony expunction. Section 99-19-71(3) governs the effect: a nonpublic record is retained by the Mississippi Criminal Information Center solely to determine first-offender status in subsequent proceedings, a district attorney's office may retain a nonpublic record for law enforcement purposes, an employer may still ask whether an order of expunction has been entered, the person is restored in contemplation of law to the status occupied before arrest or indictment, and the person is not guilty of perjury for failing to recite the arrest except when first-offender status is being determined.

exclusions: None stated in subsection (4). There is no offence list, no waiting period and no first-offender requirement on this track.
A conviction. A case that ended in a conviction belongs on the first-offender misdemeanour track, the felony track, or one of the special-route tracks.
A nonadjudication dismissal, whose routing between § 99-15-26 and § 99-19-71(4) is unresolved and which is handled on its own track rather than pleaded here.
A pretrial-intervention or intervention-court completion, which produces its own disposition and is handled on the diversion node.

waitingPeriods.duration: None. Subsection (4) imposes no waiting period, no completion requirement and no clean-record condition.

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Criminal Record, LegalEase-drafted to the statute. Caption: IN THE [JUSTICE / COUNTY / CIRCUIT / MUNICIPAL] COURT OF [COUNTY] COUNTY, MISSISSIPPI; STATE OF MISSISSIPPI VS. [NAME], PETITIONER; CAUSE NO. [number]. Court, county, cause number and prosecuting authority are participant-data fields, never hardcoded. The identifying block carries date of birth, charge, offence date, arrest date, arresting agency, agency case number, disposition date and judgment of court. Race is NOT collected: no statute requires it and it is not inherited from the 2020 Fourth District model. The disposition is pleaded in the statute's own terms — that an arrest was made and the petitioner was released and the case was dismissed, OR the charges were dropped, OR there was no disposition, OR the petitioner was found not guilty at trial — and only the one that is true is pleaded. The petition quotes § 99-19-71(4) directly, including the mandatory 'shall expunge', which is safe because it is the statute rather than a characterization.

Proposed order tendered with the petition, which is Mississippi practice and is what both archived Fourth District document pairs do. Mirrors the caption. Carries the finding line as a proposal, the expungement direction to all persons and agencies keeping official records including the arresting agency, the sheriff's department and the court, the express exception for fingerprint records, the restoration and perjury-protection language, the judge's signature line, and an APPROVED AS TO FORM block for the prosecuting authority. The agency list is a set of fillable fields, never hardcoded county names.

Certificate of service reciting delivery of a true and correct copy of the petition and proposed order to the prosecuting authority by United States mail or hand delivery, with a date. The recipient and address are participant-data fields: the district attorney for the circuit district, or the county or municipal prosecuting attorney for lower courts. Never the Greenville address by default. The conviction model's certificate, which is captioned for the dismissal petition, is not reused.

Exhibit checklist. The disposition or sentencing order is attached in every case. The indictment is attached ONLY where the case was actually indicted; the Fourth District models make that allegation mandatory and that is wrong for most misdemeanours and for cases dismissed before indictment. LegalEase names each exhibit and the participant obtains and attaches it; nothing is inspected or authenticated.

Participant instructions covering: identify the correct court and county first, because Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements; request the file, docket sheet and account balance sheet from that clerk; call the clerk before filing to ask whether that court has its own preferred form or additional requirements, because Mississippi has no statewide form and practice varies by county and circuit district; file with the clerk and pay the filing fee, which the participant confirms with the clerk because no amount is published here; serve the prosecuting authority and keep the certificate; expect that some districts want the district attorney to approve the order as to form before the judge signs, which is a negotiation LegalEase does not conduct; and after the order issues, obtain certified copies and distribute them to every agency named in the order. The instructions state plainly that fingerprint records are excepted, that the Criminal Information Center keeps a nonpublic record for first-offender determinations, and that an employer may still ask whether an order of expunction was entered.

participantInputs.question: What is your full legal name, and any other name the case is under?
What is your date of birth?
What is your current address, phone number and email?
Which Mississippi county and city do you live in?

Which court handled the case — justice court, county court, circuit court, or municipal court? Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements and people routinely misidentify which one heard their case.
Which county was that court in? For a municipal court, which city?
What is the cause or case number?
What were you charged with, and under which Mississippi Code section if you know it?
On what date did the offence happen?
On what date were you arrested or cited?
Which agency arrested or cited you, and what is their case number if you have it?
Which prosecuting authority handled the case — the district attorney for the circuit district, or a county or municipal prosecuting attorney?

How did the case end? Choose the one that matches: you were arrested and released and the case was dismissed; the charges were dropped; there was never any disposition; or you were found not guilty at trial.
On what date did that happen?
Was the case ever presented to a grand jury and indicted? Many cases are not, and the petition only pleads an indictment where one exists.
What exactly does your paperwork say about how the case ended? Copy the wording. Phrases like 'passed to the file' or 'retired to the file' need a closer look before we go further.
Was this a nonadjudication, a pretrial intervention programme, or an intervention or drug court? Those end differently and route differently.
Was anyone charged with you whose case is still open?

rules.filing: File the petition with the proposed order and certificate of service with the clerk of the justice, county, circuit or municipal court in which the case was pending. Mississippi has no statewide form; the petition is drafted to the statute and the court, county and prosecuting authority are participant data. Call the clerk before filing to ask whether that court has its own preferred form or additional requirements.
rules.fees: No amount is published here. Section 99-19-72 sets a fee for a petition to expunge an offence under § 99-19-71, and subsection (4) sits inside § 99-19-71, but charging a person whose case was dismissed is a contested result and county practice differs. The participant is instructed to confirm the filing fee with the clerk before filing. See the unresolved fee question.
rules.feeWaiver: A pauper's affidavit under general Mississippi practice. Not verified for expungement specifically; the participant asks the clerk.
rules.notice: The prosecuting authority receives a copy. The ten days' written notice to the district attorney is imposed by § 99-19-71(2)(b), which sits inside the felony conviction subsection, and it is NOT imported into this subsection without textual support; the packet nonetheless tells the participant that some districts expect notice and prosecutor approval as a matter of local practice. No response or objection period is stated for this track and no hearing is required by subsection (4).
rules.service: United States mail or hand delivery by the petitioner to the prosecuting authority, contemporaneous with filing, evidenced by the certificate of service.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank and does not use the archived models' 'by and through his attorney' recital.
rules.notarization: Required. The petition carries the specification's VERIFICATION section — a verification on oath with a jurat, notarisationRequired true — as packet specification MS-nonconviction-expungement-99-19-71-4 (v2.0.0) requires and as the owner direction of 2026-09-03 confirmed when the Clinic Mode participant-delivery PDFs were reviewed with their verification and notarization blanks unsigned. The archived Fourth District models' lack of a verification is a drafting-reference observation and no longer governs the packet. unresolvedQuestions.question: Whether the Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-72 fee reaches a given petition. The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk. Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

tracks.legalName: First-Offender Misdemeanor Conviction Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(1))

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 99-19-71(1), read from the enrolled text of 2026 HB 1546, provides: 'Any person who has been convicted of a misdemeanor that is not a traffic violation, and who is a first offender, may petition the justice, county, circuit or municipal court in which the conviction was had for an order to expunge any such conviction from all public records.' Subsection (1) contains NO waiting period, no completion requirement and no pending-charge restriction — the payment condition sits in subsection (2)(a) and is written for the felony track. Relief is permissive as to petitioning ('may petition') and the statute does not say the court shall grant, so it is treated as discretionary. Two elements carry the whole eligibility test: the offence must not be a traffic violation, and the person must be a first offender. Section 99-19-71(3) resolves what 'first offender' has to survive: a nonpublic record of every expunction is retained by the Mississippi Criminal Information Center 'solely for the purpose of determining whether, in subsequent proceedings, the person is a first offender', and the section's own perjury protection is expressly disapplied 'for the purpose of determining, in any subsequent proceedings under this section, whether the person is a first offender'. A previously expunged conviction therefore remains available to defeat first-offender status on a later petition, and the participant may not deny it for that purpose.

exclusions: A traffic violation. The statute reaches 'a misdemeanor that is not a traffic violation', and many Mississippi misdemeanours sit near that line.

A person who is not a first offender. A previously expunged conviction remains available to the Criminal Information Center under § 99-19-71(3) precisely to determine first-offender status in subsequent proceedings, so an earlier expunction does not restore first-offender status.
DUI, which has its own route and must never be handled here.
A felony, which is subsection (2).

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Criminal Record, LegalEase-drafted to the statute. Caption: IN THE [JUSTICE / COUNTY / CIRCUIT / MUNICIPAL] COURT OF [COUNTY] COUNTY, MISSISSIPPI; STATE OF MISSISSIPPI VS. [NAME], PETITIONER; CAUSE NO. [number]. Court, county, cause number and prosecuting authority are participant-data fields, never hardcoded. The identifying block carries date of birth, charge, offence date, arrest date, arresting agency, agency case number, disposition date and judgment of court. Race is NOT collected: no statute requires it and it is not inherited from the 2020 Fourth District model. The petition pleads the conviction, that the offence is a misdemeanour and is not a traffic violation, and that the petitioner is a first offender — the last as the participant's own assertion, never as a LegalEase certification.

Proposed order tendered with the petition, which is Mississippi practice and is what both archived Fourth District document pairs do. Mirrors the caption. Carries the finding line as a proposal, the expungement direction to all persons and agencies keeping official records including the arresting agency, the sheriff's department and the court, the express exception for fingerprint records, the restoration and perjury-protection language, the judge's signature line, and an APPROVED AS TO FORM block for the prosecuting authority. The agency list is a set of fillable fields, never hardcoded county names.

Certificate of service reciting delivery of a true and correct copy of the petition and proposed order to the prosecuting authority by United States mail or hand delivery, with a date. The recipient and address are participant-data fields: the district attorney for the circuit district, or the county or municipal prosecuting attorney for lower courts. Never the Greenville address by default. The conviction model's certificate, which is captioned for the dismissal petition, is not reused.

Exhibit checklist. The disposition or sentencing order is attached in every case. The indictment is attached ONLY where the case was actually indicted; the Fourth District models make that allegation mandatory and that is wrong for most misdemeanours and for cases dismissed before indictment. LegalEase names each exhibit and the participant obtains and attaches it; nothing is inspected or authenticated.

Participant instructions covering: identify the correct court and county first, because Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements; request the file, docket sheet and account balance sheet from that clerk; call the clerk before filing to ask whether that court has its own preferred form or additional requirements, because Mississippi has no statewide form and practice varies by county and circuit district; file with the clerk and pay the filing fee, which the participant confirms with the clerk because no amount is published here; serve the prosecuting authority and keep the certificate; expect that some districts want the district attorney to approve the order as to form before the judge signs, which is a negotiation LegalEase does not conduct; and after the order issues, obtain certified copies and distribute them to every agency named in the order. The instructions state plainly that fingerprint records are excepted, that the Criminal Information Center keeps a nonpublic record for first-offender determinations, and that an employer may still ask whether an order of expunction was entered.

participantInputs.question: What is your full legal name, and any other name the case is under?
What is your date of birth?
What is your current address, phone number and email?
Which Mississippi county and city do you live in?

Which court handled the case — justice court, county court, circuit court, or municipal court? Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements and people routinely misidentify which one heard their case.
Which county was that court in? For a municipal court, which city?
What is the cause or case number?
What were you charged with, and under which Mississippi Code section if you know it?
On what date did the offence happen?
On what date were you arrested or cited?
Which agency arrested or cited you, and what is their case number if you have it?
Which prosecuting authority handled the case — the district attorney for the circuit district, or a county or municipal prosecuting attorney?
On what date were you convicted?
Was the offence a misdemeanour?
Was the offence a traffic violation? Traffic violations cannot be expunged on this route, and some Mississippi misdemeanours sit close to that line.
Was the offence a DUI? DUI has its own separate route and is never handled here.
Have you ever been convicted of any other offence, in any Mississippi court or anywhere else?

Have you ever had any conviction expunged before? An earlier expungement does not give you first-offender status back: the Criminal Information Center keeps a nonpublic record specifically so a court can tell whether you are a first offender.
Are all fines, costs and restitution on this case paid in full?

unresolvedQuestions.question: Whether the Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-72 fee reaches a given petition. The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk. Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

Both the review and the Fourth District materials establish that districts maintain their own petition and order preferences and that some expect the district attorney to sign the order as approved as to form before the judge will sign. This is a scaling constraint rather than a legal one: the statutory mechanism is the same statewide, but the accepted document and the practical gate vary. unresolvedQuestions.question: Trafficking-survivor relief under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-54.6, as amended by 2026 HB 1546 effective 1 July 2026, is recorded here as a separately-listed matter and NOT as a tenth normalized source node, because neither the adopted Batch 2 memorandum nor the authoritative source crosswalk lists it among Mississippi's nine core adult slots. The enrolled text was read: new § 97-3-54.6(6) lets the sentencing court, at any time after a conviction or adjudication of delinquency of a misdemeanour or a felony not classified as a crime of violence under § 97-3-2, expunge on appropriate motion where it finds by a preponderance that participation in the offence occurred during the period the person was being trafficked and was the direct result of that trafficking; official documentation from a federal, state or local government agency creates a presumption but is not required; and new § 97-3-54.6(7)(b) provides that neither failing to raise the trafficking affirmative defence nor the court's finding on it affects the ability to file under subsection (6). This relief is broader and faster than ordinary § 99-19-71 conviction expungement, so screening for it belongs on every intake. Whether it becomes a normalized node requires an express crosswalk or memorandum instruction.

provenance.sourceStatement: this relief is easier to obtain than ordinary misdemeanor conviction expungement under § 99-19-71, which is limited to first offenders and carries waiting periods and court-debt payment requirements. For a survivor, the trafficking route is both broader and faster. Wilma should be screening for it, gently, on every intake, not treating it as an edge case.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review approved this track with limitations and the enrolled text confirms subsection (1) unchanged. It is custom_pleading for the same reason as every Mississippi petition track: no statewide form exists and the statute prescribes none. The review's build blocker on whether an expunged prior defeats first-offender status is CLOSED by the enrolled text: § 99-19-71(3) retains a nonpublic record with the Criminal Information Center solely to determine first-offender status in subsequent proceedings, and the perjury protection is expressly disapplied for that determination, so an earlier expunction does not restore first-offender status and the participant may not deny it for that purpose. That rule is encoded precisely. No waiting period is invented, because subsection (1) contains none. First-offender status and traffic classification are the participant's own assertions and are never certified by LegalEase.

limitations.statement: Mississippi has no statewide expungement form and § 99-19-71 prescribes none. The four archived petition and order PDFs are Fourth Circuit Court District models covering Leflore, Sunflower and Washington counties only: every county field reads '(Washington, Sunflower, or Leflore)', the certificate of service hardcodes the Fourth District DA at Greenville, the signature blocks are dated 2020, and the orders carry an APPROVED AS TO FORM block. They are drafting references only. Court, county and prosecuting authority are participant-data fields and are never hardcoded.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge One Felony Conviction (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(2), as amended by 2026 HB 1546)

controllingAuthority.summary: Read from the ENROLLED text of 2026 HB 1546, which amends § 99-19-71 and took effect 1 July 2026. Subsection (2)(a): except as otherwise provided in the subsection, a person convicted of a felony who has paid all criminal fines and costs of court imposed in the sentence of conviction may petition the court in which the conviction was had for an order to expunge ONE conviction from all public records THREE (3) YEARS after the successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence, upon a hearing as determined in the discretion of the court. HB 1546 struck 'five (5)' and inserted 'three (3)'. Twelve categories are ineligible: a crime of violence under § 97-3-2; arson, first degree under §§ 97-17-1 and 97-17-3; trafficking in controlled substances under § 41-29-139; a third, fourth or subsequent offence DUI under § 63-11-30(2)(c) and (2)(d); felon in possession of a firearm under § 97-37-5; failure to register as a sex offender under § 45-33-33; voyeurism under § 97-29-61; witness intimidation under § 97-9-113; abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable person under § 43-47-19; embezzlement under §§ 97-11-25 and 97-23-19; and, NEWLY ADDED BY HB 1546, felony procuring prostitution under § 97-29-51 and promoting prostitution under § 97-29-51. A person is eligible for only one felony expunction under paragraph (a), and the enrolled text now defines the terms: 'one (1) conviction' and 'one (1) felony expunction' mean and include all convictions that arose from a COMMON NUCLEUS OF OPERATIVE FACTS as determined in the discretion of the court. Subsection (2)(b): the petitioner shall give ten (10) days' written notice to the district attorney before any hearing; the court may grant if it determines, on the record or in writing, that the applicant is rehabilitated from the offence; and where the court denies, its findings must be identified specifically and not generally. Subsection (5): no public official is eligible for expunction under the section for any conviction related to his official duties. HB 1546 carries no applicability clause limiting it to convictions or petitions after a given date; SECTION 4 provides only that the act takes effect from and after 1 July 2026.

exclusions: A crime of violence as provided in Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-2. This is a defined list and it is long.

Voyeurism as provided in § 97-29-61.

Embezzlement as provided in §§ 97-11-25 and 97-23-19.

Promoting prostitution as provided in § 97-29-51 — ADDED by 2026 HB 1546 effective 1 July 2026.
A public official, for any conviction related to his official duties (§ 99-19-71(5)).
A person who has already had one felony expunction under paragraph (a). The allowance is once per lifetime.

participantInputs.question: What is your full legal name, and any other name the case is under?
What is your date of birth?
What is your current address, phone number and email?
Which Mississippi county and city do you live in?

Which court handled the case — justice court, county court, circuit court, or municipal court? Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements and people routinely misidentify which one heard their case.
Which county was that court in? For a municipal court, which city?
What is the cause or case number?
What were you charged with, and under which Mississippi Code section if you know it?
On what date did the offence happen?
On what date were you arrested or cited?
Which agency arrested or cited you, and what is their case number if you have it?
Which prosecuting authority handled the case — the district attorney for the circuit district, or a county or municipal prosecuting attorney?
On what date were you convicted of the felony?
What felony were you convicted of, and under which Mississippi Code section?
What did your sentence include — incarceration, probation, supervised release, fines, costs, restitution, treatment, or a combination?
On what date did you successfully complete the LAST of all those terms and conditions? Not the conviction date and not your release date.
Are all criminal fines and costs of court imposed in the sentence paid in full? This is a separate statutory condition.

Is your conviction any of these: a crime of violence under § 97-3-2; first-degree arson; trafficking in controlled substances; a third or subsequent DUI; felon in possession of a firearm; failure to register as a sex offender; voyeurism; witness intimidation; abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable person; embezzlement; felony procuring prostitution; or promoting prostitution?
Have you ever had a felony conviction expunged in Mississippi before? You are eligible for only one felony expunction in your lifetime.

Were you convicted of more than one felony out of the same set of events? Mississippi counts all convictions arising from a common nucleus of operative facts as ONE conviction and ONE expunction, and the court decides that in its discretion.
Were you a public official, and was the conviction related to your official duties?
In your own words, what have you done since the offence? The court has to decide whether you are rehabilitated, and this is your statement, not ours. A lawyer should review it before you file.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review returned this track as 'additional research required' on a single urgent question, and the enrolled text of 2026 HB 1546 closes it. The bill DOES amend § 99-19-71: its long title is 'AN ACT TO AMEND SECTION 99-19-71 ... TO REVISE EXPUNCTION OF CRIMINAL RECORD BY REDUCING THE WAITING PERIOD FOR ELIGIBILITY; TO PROHIBIT THE EXPUNGEMENT OF THE FELONY CRIMES OF PROMOTING OR PROCURING PROSTITUTION', and the amendment markup strikes 'five (5)' and inserts 'three (3)'. The waiting period is therefore THREE years from 1 July 2026, and felony procuring prostitution and promoting prostitution under § 97-29-51 are newly excluded. The review's contrary suspicion — that HB 1546 touched only § 97-3-54.6 — is not borne out; the bill amends §§ 99-19-71, 97-3-54.1 and 97-3-54.6 together. The enrolled text also closes two further open questions: 'one (1) conviction' and 'one (1) felony expunction' are defined to include all convictions arising from a common nucleus of operative facts as determined in the court's discretion, and the ten-day district attorney notice now sits at subsection (2)(b). The track is custom_pleading because Mississippi has no statewide form. The discretionary rehabilitation finding, the ten-day notice and the hearing are packet instructions and post-generation handoff, not reasons to withhold the petition; the rehabilitation showing is participant-authored and attorney-reviewed and is never composed by LegalEase.

tracks.publicName: Clearing additional misdemeanors in city or justice court

controllingAuthority.summary: Two parallel provisions give the lower courts a discretionary power to expunge their own misdemeanour convictions: § 9-11-15(3) for justice court and § 21-23-7(6) for municipal court. They share one mechanism, one filing vehicle and one legal effect and differ only in which court is petitioned and which prosecutor is noticed, so they are modelled as ONE node with two venue branches rather than split. The complete text of both was obtained and compared word for word: every operative element is identical and the only differences are the court petitioned, the prosecutor noticed, clause order and pronoun style. Section 9-11-15(3) was added by Laws 2016 ch. 406 § 1 as a copy of the then-existing municipal provision; § 21-23-7(6) was last amended by Laws 2021 ch. 356. The court may, in its discretion, expunge the record of conviction of any or all misdemeanours in THAT court, on a showing made in open court of (i) rehabilitation, (ii) good conduct for two years since the last conviction in ANY court, and (iii) that the best interest of society would be served. The two-year clock runs from the last conviction in any court, not merely in the petitioned court, so a criminal-history check rather than self-report is required. Each court expunges only its own misdemeanours, so a participant with convictions in two municipal courts needs two petitions. The order does not apply to the confidential records of law-enforcement agencies and has NO effect on the driving record maintained under Title 63. Relief is expressly discretionary. Section 99-19-72's fee applies by its terms to petitions under § 99-19-71 and does not reach these sections.

exclusions: Convictions entered in any court other than the one petitioned. Each court expunges only its own misdemeanours.
The confidential records of law-enforcement agencies, which the order does not reach.
The driving record maintained under Title 63, which is expressly unaffected.
A participant who has been convicted of anything in any court within the last two years, because the good-conduct period runs from the last conviction in any court.
Felonies, and DUI, which have their own routes.

controllingAuthority.summary: Under § 99-15-26 the court withholds acceptance of a guilty plea and sentence, imposes conditions, and on successful completion directs that the cause be dismissed and the case closed. Expungement of the resulting record is available on petition under the section's expungement subsection, which the retained review identifies as § 99-15-26(5). The complete text was obtained on this pass. Subsection (1)(a) excludes crimes against the person, a crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2, a violation of § 97-11-31, and crimes in which a person unlawfully takes, obtains or misappropriates funds received by or entrusted to them by virtue of public office or employment; subsection (1)(d) additionally excludes trafficking under § 41-29-139(f) and every offence under the Implied Consent Law, which can only be nonadjudicated under § 63-11-30, and makes the benefit ONCE-ONLY. unresolvedQuestions.question: The complete current text of Miss. Code Ann. § 99-15-26 was obtained on this pass and resolves most of what the review left open. The section is the integration of two 2019 acts under § 1-1-109 — Laws 2019 ch. 362 § 4 and Laws 2019 ch. 466 § 41, the Criminal Justice Reform Act — with no enacted amendment since. Subsection (1)(a) covers felony and misdemeanour cases in circuit or county court on a guilty plea entered on or after 1 July 2014, OTHER THAN crimes against the person, a crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2, a violation of § 97-11-31, or crimes in which a person unlawfully takes, obtains or misappropriates funds received by or entrusted to the person by virtue of public office or employment; (1)(b) covers misdemeanours in justice or municipal court; (1)(c) covers misdemeanour domestic violence in any of the four courts. Subsection (1)(d) makes the benefit ONCE-ONLY — 'No person having previously qualified under the provisions of this section shall be eligible to qualify for release in accordance with this section for a repeat offense' — and excludes trafficking under § 41-29-139(f) and any offence under the Implied Consent Law, which can only be nonadjudicated under § 63-11-30. Subsection (2) sets the conditions the court may impose, with good behaviour up to five years in circuit or county court and two years in justice or municipal court. Subsection (4) makes the DISMISSAL automatic: on successful completion the court 'shall direct that the cause be dismissed and the case be closed'. The expungement subsection is (5) as the review recorded, and it requires a petition. One textual gap survives and is preserved rather than resolved: § 99-15-26(5) and § 99-19-71(4) are near-verbatim twins, and BOTH are keyed to 'a case in which an arrest was made, the person arrested was released and the case was dismissed', which describes a pre-adjudication arrest-and-release posture rather than a post-guilty-plea nonadjudication dismissal under (4). Neither section says in terms that a subsection (4) dismissal is expungeable on petition.

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 63-11-30 carries its own first-offence DUI expungement provision, entirely separate from the ordinary misdemeanour route, and a DUI must never be routed through § 99-19-71(1). Every condition must be met: at least five years after successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence; the person did not hold a commercial driver's licence or a commercial learner's permit at the time of the offence; the person did not refuse the blood or breath test; blood alcohol concentration below .16 where test results are available; no other DUI conviction and no pending DUI; the person has not previously had a DUI nonadjudication or a DUI expungement; and the person must justify the expungement to the court. Relief is discretionary. Venue is the CIRCUIT COURT of the county of conviction: the Attorney General has opined that a municipal court judge is not authorized to expunge a DUI conviction, although municipal and justice courts may handle expungement of nonadjudicated first-offence DUI charges in certain circumstances. That is the most likely way a Mississippi DUI petition gets filed in the wrong court. A third, fourth or subsequent DUI under § 63-11-30(2)(c) and (2)(d) is separately excluded from felony expungement under § 99-19-71(2)(a)(iv). The complete current text was obtained on this pass from enrolled SB 2095 (Laws 2022 ch. 303), the last enacted amendment: the expungement provision is subsection (13), captioned 'Expunction'. It is frequently cited in practice as § 63-11-30(14); per the 2022 enrolled act (13) is Expunction and (14) is Nonadjudication. Subsection (13)(b) additionally makes a person eligible for only ONE expunction under the subsection and directs the Department of Public Safety to maintain a permanent confidential registry of all such expunctions solely to determine eligibility for expunction, for nonadjudication, or as a first offender. Subsection (13)(c) requires the court to state in writing the justification for which the expunction was granted and to forward the order to the Department of Public Safety within five days.

exclusions: A person who held a commercial driver's licence or a commercial learner's permit at the time of the offence.
A person who refused the blood or breath test.
A blood alcohol concentration of .16 or above where test results are available.
Any other DUI conviction, and any pending DUI.
A person who has previously had a DUI nonadjudication or a DUI expungement.
A second, third, fourth or subsequent DUI. Third and subsequent DUI under § 63-11-30(2)(c) and (2)(d) is also excluded from felony expungement under § 99-19-71(2)(a)(iv).
Filing anywhere other than the circuit court of the county of conviction. A municipal court judge is not authorized to expunge a DUI conviction.

tracks.publicName: Cases you resolved through a program

controllingAuthority.summary: The complete text of both provisions was obtained on this pass, and it splits this slot into two legally distinct branches rather than one. PRETRIAL INTERVENTION, § 99-15-123 (last amended Laws 2008 ch. 444 § 1): subsection (1) makes the DISPOSITION automatic — on successful completion 'the court shall make a noncriminal disposition of the charge or charges', which § 99-15-103 defines as dismissal of the charge without prejudice to reinstatement on the district attorney's motion — but subsection (3) makes the EXPUNGEMENT petition-based: 'Upon petition therefor, the court shall expunge the record of any case in which an arrest was made, the person arrested was released and the case was dismissed or the charges were dropped or there was no disposition of such case.' The court's duty is mandatory once petitioned, but no order enters without the petition. Note subsection (3) omits the 'found not guilty at trial' limb that § 99-19-71(4) contains. INTERVENTION COURT, § 9-23-23 (last amended by 2019 HB 1352 § 13, which substituted 'intervention' for 'drug' and inserted 'and not waived by the court'): 'If the participant completes all requirements imposed upon him by the intervention court, including the payment of fines and fees assessed and not waived by the court, the charge and prosecution shall be dismissed. If the defendant or participant was sentenced at the time of entry of plea of guilty, the successful completion of the intervention court order and other requirements of probation or suspension of sentence will result in the record of the criminal conviction or adjudication being expunged. However, no expunction of any implied consent violation shall be allowed.' That section contains NO petition language, no application requirement, no fee, no hearing, no notice and no waiting period — unlike §§ 99-19-71, 99-15-26(5), 99-15-123(3), 41-29-150(d)(2) and 63-11-30(13), every one of which expressly requires a petition or application. Its expungement language is the most self-executing in the Mississippi scheme.

An implied consent violation, which § 9-23-23 expressly bars from expunction in intervention court and which routes to the DUI track under § 63-11-30 instead.
The programme itself is not record-clearance relief. It produces a disposition; only the § 99-15-123(3) petition, or the § 9-23-23 result, clears a record.

units.label: Pretrial intervention — § 99-15-123(3) petition to expunge
units.description: The petition branch. Successful completion of pretrial intervention produces a noncriminal disposition automatically under § 99-15-123(1) — the court 'shall make' it, and no participant filing is involved — but the expungement of the resulting record does NOT follow automatically. Section 99-15-123(3) provides expungement 'Upon petition therefor', and the court's duty is mandatory only once the petition is filed. That is a distinct participant request for relief with its own statutory basis, its own destination and its own legal output, which is why this slot carries a genuine relief branch rather than verification alone. LegalEase drafts the petition, the proposed order and the certificate of service to § 99-15-123(3), pleading the pretrial intervention, its successful completion, the noncriminal disposition and its date. The pleaded category is taken from subsection (3)'s own terms, which reach a case in which an arrest was made and the person was released and the case was dismissed, or the charges were dropped, or there was no disposition — and which, unlike § 99-19-71(4), do NOT include a finding of not guilty at trial.

units.label: Intervention court — verification of the self-executing result, and routing
units.description: The verification branch. Section 9-23-23 states a result rather than a procedure: on completion of all requirements the charge and prosecution 'shall be dismissed', and where the person was sentenced at the time of the guilty plea completion 'will result in the record of the criminal conviction or adjudication being expunged'. There is no petition language, no application, no fee, no hearing, no notice and no waiting period anywhere in the section — which is unique in the Mississippi scheme and is why no petition is generated on this branch. The section does not, however, direct any officer to enter or transmit an order, so whether an expungement order in fact issues without the participant asking is a matter of local practice and is preserved as an open question. The correct product output is therefore verification: establish from the clerk what was actually entered and when, obtain a certified copy of any dismissal or expungement order that already exists, and route onward only where the record shows relief did not issue. Implied consent violations are expressly barred from expunction here and route to the DUI track.

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Criminal Record, LegalEase-drafted to the statute. Caption: IN THE [JUSTICE / COUNTY / CIRCUIT / MUNICIPAL] COURT OF [COUNTY] COUNTY, MISSISSIPPI; STATE OF MISSISSIPPI VS. [NAME], PETITIONER; CAUSE NO. [number]. Court, county, cause number and prosecuting authority are participant-data fields, never hardcoded. The identifying block carries date of birth, charge, offence date, arrest date, arresting agency, agency case number, disposition date and judgment of court. Race is NOT collected: no statute requires it and it is not inherited from the 2020 Fourth District model. On the pretrial intervention branch the petition is drafted to § 99-15-123(3) alone. It pleads the pretrial intervention agreement, its successful completion, the resulting noncriminal disposition and its date, and the statutory category from subsection (3)'s own terms. It does not cite § 99-19-71 unless the participant separately and genuinely qualifies under subsection (4) as well.

Proposed order tendered with the petition, which is Mississippi practice and is what both archived Fourth District document pairs do. Mirrors the caption. Carries the finding line as a proposal, the expungement direction to all persons and agencies keeping official records including the arresting agency, the sheriff's department and the court, the express exception for fingerprint records, the restoration and perjury-protection language, the judge's signature line, and an APPROVED AS TO FORM block for the prosecuting authority. The agency list is a set of fillable fields, never hardcoded county names.

Certificate of service reciting delivery of a true and correct copy of the petition and proposed order to the prosecuting authority by United States mail or hand delivery, with a date. The recipient and address are participant-data fields: the district attorney for the circuit district, or the county or municipal prosecuting attorney for lower courts. Never the Greenville address by default. The conviction model's certificate, which is captioned for the dismissal petition, is not reused.

Exhibit checklist. The disposition or sentencing order is attached in every case. The indictment is attached ONLY where the case was actually indicted; the Fourth District models make that allegation mandatory and that is wrong for most misdemeanours and for cases dismissed before indictment. LegalEase names each exhibit and the participant obtains and attaches it; nothing is inspected or authenticated.

Participant instructions covering: identify the correct court and county first, because Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements; request the file, docket sheet and account balance sheet from that clerk; call the clerk before filing to ask whether that court has its own preferred form or additional requirements, because Mississippi has no statewide form and practice varies by county and circuit district; file with the clerk and pay the filing fee, which the participant confirms with the clerk because no amount is published here; serve the prosecuting authority and keep the certificate; expect that some districts want the district attorney to approve the order as to form before the judge signs, which is a negotiation LegalEase does not conduct; and after the order issues, obtain certified copies and distribute them to every agency named in the order. The instructions state plainly that fingerprint records are excepted, that the Criminal Information Center keeps a nonpublic record for first-offender determinations, and that an employer may still ask whether an order of expunction was entered.

The intervention court verification branch and the routing layer for both. It establishes which statute applies, whether the person was sentenced at the time of the guilty plea, and — critically — whether relief has ALREADY been entered, because § 9-23-23 states its result without prescribing a procedure and participants frequently have an order they do not hold a copy of. It supplies the clerk-contact script, the document checklist, and the routing decision: petition under § 99-15-123(3) on the pretrial intervention branch; certified copy and distribution checklist where an intervention court order already exists; and onward routing where the record shows relief did not issue. It states plainly that the programme itself is not record-clearance relief and that no petition is generated on the intervention court branch.

tracks.legalName: Controlled-Substance Conditional Discharge and Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-29-150)

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 41-29-150 carries Mississippi's controlled-substance conditional discharge and its associated expungement. A first-time eligible drug possession or paraphernalia case may be handled WITHOUT entering a judgment of guilt: the court defers proceedings, places the person on probation, and on successful completion discharges the person and dismisses the proceedings without an adjudication of guilt. Expungement of the record is then available on application to the court. The benefit is once-only, and a nonpublic record is retained for future eligibility checks, which is the same design as the § 99-19-71(3) first-offender retention. Trafficking under § 41-29-139 is a separate offence and is outside this route entirely; it is also independently excluded from felony expungement under § 99-19-71(2)(a)(iii). The complete current text was obtained on this pass, from the last enacted amendment, Laws 2010 ch. 460 § 2. The conditional discharge is § 41-29-150(d)(1) and the expungement remedy is § 41-29-150(d)(2). Eligibility reaches a person NOT previously convicted of violating § 41-29-139, or the laws of the United States or another state relating to narcotic drugs, stimulant or depressant substances, other controlled substances or marihuana, who is found guilty of a violation of § 41-29-139(c) or (d) — simple possession and paraphernalia — after trial or on a plea. The court may, without entering a judgment of guilt and with the person's consent, defer further proceedings and place them on probation for not more than three years; if no condition is violated, on expiry the court SHALL discharge the person and dismiss the proceedings, without adjudication of guilt. Discharge and dismissal may occur ONLY ONCE with respect to any person, and a nonpublic record is retained by the Bureau of Narcotics solely for the courts to determine whether the person qualifies again. Under (d)(2) the person may then APPLY to the court for an expungement order; the court determines the matter AFTER HEARING and, on the requisite findings, SHALL enter the order. Section 41-29-150 specifies no fee.

exclusions: Trafficking, sale, distribution and manufacture under § 41-29-139(a) and § 41-29-139(f). This route reaches only violations of § 41-29-139(c), simple possession, and § 41-29-139(d), paraphernalia.

tracks.legalName: Underage Alcohol Possession Expungement (Miss. Code Ann. § 67-3-70)

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 67-3-70 governs underage alcohol offences and carries its own expungement provision at subsection (6). The complete current text was obtained on this pass from enrolled HB 917 § 34 (Laws 2020 ch. 314), the last enacted amendment, so the one-year period is now supported by PRIMARY authority rather than by the secondary clearinghouse source the review relied on. Subsection (6) reads: 'Any person who has been charged with a violation of subsections (1) or (2) of this section may, not sooner than one (1) year after the dismissal and discharge or completion of any sentence and/or payment of any fine, apply to the court for an order to expunge from all official records all recordation relating to his arrest, trial, finding or plea of guilty, and dismissal and discharge. If the court determines that such person was dismissed and the proceedings against him discharged or that such person had satisfactorily served his sentence and/or paid his fine, it shall enter such order.' Four consequences follow. The route reaches subsections (1) and (2) only — underage purchase or possession of light wine, light spirit product or beer, and an underage false-age statement or false document — and does not reach subsection (3), furnishing to a minor. It reaches anyone 'CHARGED WITH' such a violation, so dismissed and discharged cases qualify as well as convictions. The one-year clock runs from the LATER of dismissal and discharge, or completion of any sentence and payment of any fine, not from the offence or the charge. And relief is MANDATORY on the findings — 'it shall enter such order' — unlike the discretionary lower-court misdemeanour route. The section prescribes no petition contents, no prosecutor notice, no open-court showing, no rehabilitation finding, no hearing and no fee, and it contains no restoration-of-status clause, no perjury-protection clause and no Title 63 carve-out.

exclusions: Offences outside § 67-3-70(1) and (2). The route reaches underage purchase or possession of light wine, light spirit product or beer, and an underage false-age statement or presentation of a false document for that purpose. It does NOT reach § 67-3-70(3), furnishing or purchasing for a minor, which is an adult offence.
DUI, which has its own route and is never handled here.

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Criminal Record, LegalEase-drafted to the statute. Caption: IN THE [JUSTICE / COUNTY / CIRCUIT / MUNICIPAL] COURT OF [COUNTY] COUNTY, MISSISSIPPI; STATE OF MISSISSIPPI VS. [NAME], PETITIONER; CAUSE NO. [number]. Court, county, cause number and prosecuting authority are participant-data fields, never hardcoded. The identifying block carries date of birth, charge, offence date, arrest date, arresting agency, agency case number, disposition date and judgment of court. Race is NOT collected: no statute requires it and it is not inherited from the 2020 Fourth District model. The petition pleads the underage alcohol charge, its disposition and the completion of any sentence, and asks the court to expunge the record under § 67-3-70. Because the waiting period is not established from primary authority, the petition does not recite an elapsed period as a statutory element; the instructions tell the participant to confirm the current rule with the clerk before filing.

Proposed order tendered with the petition, which is Mississippi practice and is what both archived Fourth District document pairs do. Mirrors the caption. Carries the finding line as a proposal, the expungement direction to all persons and agencies keeping official records including the arresting agency, the sheriff's department and the court, the express exception for fingerprint records, the restoration and perjury-protection language, the judge's signature line, and an APPROVED AS TO FORM block for the prosecuting authority. The agency list is a set of fillable fields, never hardcoded county names.

Certificate of service reciting delivery of a true and correct copy of the petition and proposed order to the prosecuting authority by United States mail or hand delivery, with a date. The recipient and address are participant-data fields: the district attorney for the circuit district, or the county or municipal prosecuting attorney for lower courts. Never the Greenville address by default. The conviction model's certificate, which is captioned for the dismissal petition, is not reused.

Exhibit checklist. The disposition or sentencing order is attached in every case. The indictment is attached ONLY where the case was actually indicted; the Fourth District models make that allegation mandatory and that is wrong for most misdemeanours and for cases dismissed before indictment. LegalEase names each exhibit and the participant obtains and attaches it; nothing is inspected or authenticated.

Participant instructions covering: identify the correct court and county first, because Mississippi has four trial court levels that all handle expungements; request the file, docket sheet and account balance sheet from that clerk; call the clerk before filing to ask whether that court has its own preferred form or additional requirements, because Mississippi has no statewide form and practice varies by county and circuit district; file with the clerk and pay the filing fee, which the participant confirms with the clerk because no amount is published here; serve the prosecuting authority and keep the certificate; expect that some districts want the district attorney to approve the order as to form before the judge signs, which is a negotiation LegalEase does not conduct; and after the order issues, obtain certified copies and distribute them to every agency named in the order. The instructions state plainly that fingerprint records are excepted, that the Criminal Information Center keeps a nonpublic record for first-offender determinations, and that an employer may still ask whether an order of expunction was entered.

The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk.
